goals: Name the three subatomic particles and state their charge, mass and place in the atom
Describe how the electron, proton and neutron were discovered
Describe the Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models with the observations behind them
State the limitation of each model

slides.heading: Structure of an Atom
slides.body_md: Part 1: the particles inside an atom, and how three models, each fixing a problem of the one before, led to the picture we use today.

rows: a neutral particle in the nucleus

visual.alt: Table of six steps in the discovery of atomic structure with the scientist, the approximate year and what was found

slides.narration: Dalton thought that an atom was a solid ball that could not be divided. Experiments with electricity showed that this was not true. In this part we meet the particles inside the atom, and then three models of the atom, each one built to fix a problem in the one before it.

slides.heading: The atom can be divided
slides.body_md: Atoms are made of three **subatomic particles**. The **electron** carries a negative charge, the **proton** a positive charge and the **neutron** no charge at all. Protons and neutrons sit together in the centre, the **nucleus**. Electrons move outside it. The charge on a proton is equal in size to the charge on an electron, and opposite in sign.

visual.alt: Table of electron, proton and neutron with symbol, charge, relative mass and location

slides.narration: An atom has three kinds of particles. The electron is negative. The proton is positive. The neutron has no charge. Protons and neutrons are packed together in the centre, which is called the nucleus, and the electrons move outside it. A proton and an electron have equal charges of opposite sign. A proton and a neutron have almost the same mass, and an electron is about eighteen hundred times lighter.

slides.heading: Cathode rays and the electron
slides.body_md: In a glass tube with a little gas at **very low pressure** and a high voltage across two metal plates, a glow appears. **Cathode rays** leave the negative plate, the cathode. J. J. Thomson (1897) showed that the beam bends towards a **positive** plate, so it is negatively charged, and that it is the same whatever gas or metal is used. These particles are the **electrons**, found in every atom.

slides.narration: Look at the top tube. When a high voltage is put across a tube holding a little gas at very low pressure, a beam leaves the negative plate, called the cathode. Thomson showed that this beam bends towards a positive plate, so the beam is negative. The same beam appears with any gas or metal, so these particles, the electrons, are found in every atom.

slides.heading: Canal rays, the proton and the neutron
slides.body_md: **Canal rays** (Goldstein, 1886) are positive rays that pass through holes in the cathode and travel the other way. They form when gas atoms lose electrons. With hydrogen gas the positive particle is the lightest, and it is called the **proton**. In 1932 James Chadwick found the **neutron**: a particle of almost the same mass as the proton but **no charge**. Because it is neutral it is hard to detect, which is why it was found last.

visual.alt: Table of the discoverer, evidence and charge for the electron, proton and neutron

slides.narration: Goldstein found rays that pass through holes in the cathode and move the other way. These canal rays are positive. They are made when gas atoms lose electrons. With hydrogen gas the positive particle is the lightest one, and it is called the proton. Later, in nineteen thirty two, Chadwick found a particle with almost the same mass as a proton but no charge. This is the neutron. Being neutral, it was the last to be found.

slides.heading: Thomson's model: the plum pudding
slides.body_md: Thomson (about 1904) knew that atoms are neutral and contain electrons. He pictured the atom as a **sphere of positive charge** with electrons **embedded** in it, like plums in a pudding or seeds in a watermelon. The total positive charge equals the total negative charge, so the atom is neutral. **Limitation:** it could not explain what Rutherford found in his gold-foil experiment.

slides.narration: Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge, with the electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding, or like seeds in a watermelon. The positive and negative charges are equal, so the atom is neutral. This model was a good first step. But it could not explain the result of the gold foil experiment which Rutherford did a few years later.

slides.heading: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment
slides.body_md: Rutherford (1911) fired fast **alpha particles** (positively charged helium nuclei) at a very thin gold foil and watched where they went. Each observation led to a conclusion.

rows: Most alpha particles went straight through
most of the atom is empty space
A few were deflected through small angles
the positive charge is concentrated in a small centre
Very few (roughly one in many thousands) bounced straight back
the centre, the nucleus, is tiny, dense and positive
Heavy alpha particles were never stopped by electrons
almost all the mass is in the nucleus

visual.alt: Table of four observations from the gold foil experiment and the conclusion drawn from each

slides.narration: Rutherford fired fast alpha particles, which are positive, at a very thin gold foil. Most went straight through, so most of the atom is empty space. A few were deflected through small angles, so the positive charge is concentrated in a small centre. Very few, roughly one in many thousands, bounced straight back. This means the centre, the nucleus, is tiny, dense and positive.

slides.heading: Scattering of alpha particles
slides.body_md: A positive alpha particle is pushed away only when it passes **very close** to the positive nucleus. Since the nucleus is so small, most particles miss it and go straight on. Rutherford concluded that electrons move around the nucleus in the large empty space, and that the **nucleus holds almost all the mass** of the atom.

slides.narration: Here is what happens. A positive alpha particle is pushed away only when it passes very close to the positive nucleus. The nucleus is so small that most particles miss it and go straight on. A few are turned through small angles, and very few meet a nucleus almost head on and bounce back. So the electrons move around the nucleus in the empty space, and the nucleus holds almost all the mass.

slides.heading: Worked example: how rare is a rebound?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In a classroom simulation of the experiment (numbers given for practice), 32 000 alpha particles are fired at a foil and 4 bounce straight back. Find the fraction that rebound, and say what it shows.

**Step 1.** Fraction $= \dfrac{4}{32000} = \dfrac{1}{8000}$, that is 1 in 8000.

**Step 2.** As a percentage, $\dfrac{4}{32000} \times 100 = 0.0125\%$.

**Step 3.** Only a tiny share meets the nucleus head on, so the nucleus takes up a tiny part of the atom's volume.

slides.heading: Rutherford's model and its limitation
slides.body_md: **Rutherford's model:** a small, dense, positive **nucleus** at the centre, with electrons revolving around it in circles, like planets round the Sun. **Limitation:** a charged particle that moves in a circle should keep losing energy as radiation. The electron should then spiral into the nucleus and the atom would collapse. But atoms are **stable**, so the model could not be complete.

the electron should spiral into the nucleus

visual.alt: Table linking a feature of the Rutherford model with the problem it faces

slides.narration: Rutherford described a small, dense, positive nucleus with electrons revolving around it, like planets round the Sun. There was a problem. A charged particle that moves in a circle should keep losing energy. The electron should then spiral into the nucleus and the atom should collapse. But atoms are stable, so the model could not be the full story.

slides.heading: Bohr's model: shells
slides.body_md: Niels Bohr (1913) fixed the problem with new ideas. (1) Electrons revolve only in certain special paths called **shells** or **energy levels**. (2) **While an electron stays in a shell it does not radiate energy**, so the shells are called stationary. (3) The shells are named K, L, M, N (or $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$) counting outwards from the nucleus, and each has a fixed energy. (4) An electron **absorbs** energy to jump to a higher shell and **emits** energy when it falls to a lower one.

visual.alt: Table of shells K, L, M and N with their n value, distance from the nucleus and energy

slides.narration: Bohr fixed the problem. He said that electrons move only in certain special paths called shells. While an electron stays in a shell, it does not radiate energy. The shells are named K, L, M and N, counting outwards, and each shell has a fixed energy. An electron absorbs energy to jump to a higher shell, and gives out energy when it falls to a lower shell.

The blue arrow shows an electron **emitting** energy as it falls from the M shell back to the L shell. Because the shells have fixed energies, only certain amounts of energy can be absorbed or emitted.

slides.heading: Worked example: how heavy are the electrons?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A carbon atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons. Taking a proton or neutron as 1 u and an electron as $\dfrac{1}{1836}$ u, find the share of the atom's mass that the electrons contribute.

**Step 1: nucleus** $= 6 + 6 = 12$ u.

**Step 2: electrons** $= 6 \times \dfrac{1}{1836} = 0.00327$ u.

**Step 3: share** $= \dfrac{0.00327}{12.003} \times 100 \approx 0.027\%$.

So the mass of an atom is almost all in the nucleus.

slides.narration: A carbon atom has six protons, six neutrons and six electrons. The protons and neutrons weigh about one unit each, so the nucleus has a mass of twelve units. Each electron is about one eighteen hundred and thirty sixth of a unit, so six electrons weigh about three thousandths of a unit. This is about three hundredths of a percent of the whole atom, so almost all the mass is in the nucleus.

slides.body_md: Each model explained what the one before could not. Bohr's model works well for hydrogen. For atoms with many electrons it is too simple, and later work gave the more complete picture used in higher classes.

slides.narration: Let us compare the three models. Thomson pictured a positive sphere with electrons inside, which explains why an atom is neutral. Rutherford found a tiny nucleus with electrons moving around it, which explains the scattering of alpha particles. Bohr added fixed shells, which explains why atoms are stable. Bohr model works well for hydrogen but is too simple for atoms with many electrons.

Cathode rays (Thomson) are electrons; canal rays (Goldstein) are positive; Chadwick found the neutron.

Each model fixed a problem of the one before.

slides.heading: Rules for filling the shells
slides.body_md: The maximum number of electrons in the shell with number $n$ is $2n^2$, so K holds 2, L holds 8, M holds 18 and N holds 32. Electrons fill the shell **nearest the nucleus first**. In the **outermost shell** there can be at most **8** electrons (2 for K). For the first 20 elements, the rule used in Class 9 is that the K shell takes 2, the L shell takes 8, the M shell takes up to 8, and any left over go to the N shell.

slides.narration: The most electrons the shell number n can hold is two times n squared. So K holds two, L holds eight, M holds eighteen and N holds thirty two. Electrons fill the shell nearest the nucleus first. The outermost shell never holds more than eight electrons. For the first twenty elements, K takes two, L takes eight, M takes up to eight, and any left over go to the N shell.

visual.caption: Valency from the outer shell.

slides.narration: Valency is the combining power of an atom. If an atom has one to four electrons in its outer shell, the valency is that number. With five to seven outer electrons, the valency is eight minus that number. A full outer shell gives valency zero, so such atoms are unreactive. Sodium has valency one, aluminium three, chlorine one and calcium two.

slides.heading: Worked example: distribution and valency
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the electron distribution and valency of phosphorus ($Z = 15$) and potassium ($Z = 19$).

**Step 1: phosphorus.** K takes 2, L takes 8, the remaining $15 - 10 = 5$ go to M. Distribution **2, 8, 5**. Outer electrons $= 5$, so valency $= 8 - 5 = 3$.

**Step 2: potassium.** K 2, L 8, M 8, and the last electron goes to N. Distribution **2, 8, 8, 1**. One outer electron, so valency $= 1$.

visual.alt: Table of the distribution, outer electrons and valency of phosphorus and potassium

slides.narration: Phosphorus has fifteen electrons. K takes two, L takes eight, and the remaining five go to M. The distribution is two, eight, five. With five outer electrons the valency is eight minus five, which is three. Potassium has nineteen electrons. K takes two, L eight, M eight, and the last one goes to the N shell. With one outer electron its valency is one.

slides.heading: Atomic number and mass number
slides.body_md: The **atomic number** $Z$ is the number of **protons** in the nucleus. It identifies the element. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons is also $Z$. The **mass number** $A$ is the number of protons **plus** neutrons, the nucleons in the nucleus. So the number of neutrons is $A - Z$. An atom of element X is written $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$, for example $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}$.

rows: given, or equal to electrons in an atom

visual.alt: Table of atomic number, mass number, neutrons and electrons with their meaning and how to find them

slides.narration: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons is the same. The mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons. So the number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number. The element sodium, with atomic number eleven and mass number twenty three, has twelve neutrons.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting particles
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the protons, neutrons and electrons in $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}$, $^{31}_{15}\text{P}$ and $^{40}_{20}\text{Ca}$.

**Step 1.** Protons $= Z$ and, in an atom, electrons $= Z$.

**Step 2.** Neutrons $= A - Z$: sodium $23 - 11 = 12$; phosphorus $31 - 15 = 16$; calcium $40 - 20 = 20$.

visual.alt: Table of protons, neutrons and electrons in sodium-23, phosphorus-31 and calcium-40

slides.narration: Protons equal the atomic number, and in an atom the electrons are equal to it too. Neutrons are the mass number minus the atomic number. Sodium has eleven protons, twelve neutrons and eleven electrons. Phosphorus has fifteen protons, sixteen neutrons and fifteen electrons. Calcium has twenty protons, twenty neutrons and twenty electrons.

slides.heading: Ions: atoms that gain or lose electrons
slides.body_md: An atom becomes an **ion** when it gains or loses electrons. The number of **protons never changes**. A **cation** is positive because the atom **lost** electrons, so electrons $= Z - \text{charge}$. An **anion** is negative because the atom **gained** electrons, so electrons $= Z + \text{charge}$. A metal such as sodium forms a cation, and a non-metal such as chlorine forms an anion. Most common ions reach a full outer shell, like the nearest noble gas.

visual.alt: Table of four ions with the change in electrons, protons, electrons and electron distribution

slides.narration: An atom becomes an ion when it gains or loses electrons. The number of protons never changes. A cation is positive, because the atom has lost electrons. An anion is negative, because the atom has gained electrons. Sodium loses one electron and becomes a cation with ten electrons. Chlorine gains one electron and becomes an anion with eighteen electrons. Most common ions have a full outer shell.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting particles in ions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the protons, neutrons and electrons in $^{27}_{13}\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $^{32}_{16}\text{S}^{2-}$.

**Step 1: aluminium ion.** Protons $= 13$, neutrons $= 27 - 13 = 14$, electrons $= 13 - 3 = 10$.

**Step 2: sulphide ion.** Protons $= 16$, neutrons $= 32 - 16 = 16$, electrons $= 16 + 2 = 18$.

visual.alt: Table of protons, neutrons and electrons in an aluminium ion and a sulphide ion

slides.narration: For the aluminium ion with charge three plus, the protons are thirteen, the neutrons are twenty seven minus thirteen, which is fourteen, and the electrons are thirteen minus three, which is ten. For the sulphide ion with charge two minus, the protons are sixteen, the neutrons are sixteen, and the electrons are sixteen plus two, which is eighteen.

slides.heading: Isotopes
slides.body_md: **Isotopes** are atoms of the **same element** (same $Z$) with **different mass numbers** (different numbers of neutrons). They have the same number of electrons, so their **chemical properties are the same**, but their physical properties, such as mass, differ. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium, deuterium and tritium. Chlorine has two common ones, $^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}$ and $^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}$.

visual.alt: Table of hydrogen and chlorine isotopes with Z, A, protons, neutrons and electrons

slides.narration: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different mass numbers. They have the same number of protons and electrons, but different numbers of neutrons. Their chemical properties are the same, because the electrons are the same, but their masses differ. Hydrogen has three isotopes, protium, deuterium and tritium. Chlorine has two common isotopes, with mass numbers thirty five and thirty seven.

slides.heading: Comparing isotopes of hydrogen
slides.body_md: All three isotopes of hydrogen have **1 proton and 1 electron**. Only the number of neutrons changes, from 0 to 1 to 2, and so the mass number changes from 1 to 2 to 3. Deuterium is also called heavy hydrogen.

slides.narration: Some isotopes are radioactive, which means that their nuclei give out radiation. Cobalt sixty is used to treat cancer and to sterilise medical equipment. Iodine one thirty one is used to find and treat problems of the thyroid gland, such as goitre. Uranium two thirty five is the fuel in nuclear reactors that make electricity. Carbon fourteen is used to estimate the age of fossils and old wood.

slides.heading: Quick check: uses of isotopes
slides.body_md: Decide which isotope is used for dating an old wooden object.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which isotope scientists use to estimate how old a fossil or a wooden object is.

slides.heading: Isobars
slides.body_md: **Isobars** are atoms of **different elements** with the **same mass number** but **different atomic numbers**. For example, argon-40 ($Z = 18$), potassium-40 ($Z = 19$) and calcium-40 ($Z = 20$) all have $A = 40$. Their number of protons differs, so they are different elements with different chemical properties.

visual.alt: Table comparing isotopes and isobars by atomic number, mass number, element, neutrons and example

slides.narration: Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number. For example, argon, potassium and calcium can all have a mass number of forty, but their atomic numbers are eighteen, nineteen and twenty. So they are different elements with different chemical properties. Remember, isotopes have the same atomic number, and isobars have the same mass number.

slides.heading: Worked example: average atomic mass
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Chlorine in nature is a mixture of $^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}$ (75 %) and $^{37}_{17}\text{Cl}$ (25 %). Find its average atomic mass.

**Step 1.** Average mass $= \dfrac{35 \times 75 + 37 \times 25}{100}$.

**Step 2.** $= \dfrac{2625 + 925}{100} = \dfrac{3550}{100} = 35.5$ u.

This is why the atomic mass of chlorine is **35.5 u**, a value that no single atom has.

visual.alt: Table of the two chlorine isotopes with mass number, abundance, contribution to the average and the average atomic mass

slides.narration: Chlorine in nature has seventy five percent of the isotope with mass number thirty five, and twenty five percent of the isotope with mass number thirty seven. Multiply each mass by its share and add. Thirty five times seventy five is two thousand six hundred and twenty five. Thirty seven times twenty five is nine hundred and twenty five. The total is three thousand five hundred and fifty, and dividing by one hundred gives thirty five point five.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Shell capacity is 2n squared; the first 20 elements fill K 2, L 8, M up to 8, then N.
Valency is the number of outer electrons (1 to 4), or 8 minus it (5 to 7); a full outer shell gives 0.
Z is the number of protons; A is protons plus neutrons; neutrons are A minus Z.
Ions have the same protons as the atom; cations lose electrons, anions gain electrons.
Isotopes: same Z, different A, same chemical properties. Isobars: same A, different Z.
Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotope masses.

visual.alt: Table summarising distribution, counting, isotopes, isobars and average mass with an example each

slides.narration: To sum up. Electrons fill shells nearest the nucleus first, and the outer electrons decide valency. The atomic number is the number of protons, and the mass number is protons plus neutrons. Ions have the same protons as their atoms but different electrons. Isotopes have the same atomic number and different mass numbers. Isobars have the same mass number and different atomic numbers.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Always show the distribution, for example 2, 8, 7, and then the valency in the next line.
For ions, say which electrons were lost or gained and show electrons equal to Z minus or plus the charge.
Write isotopes and isobars in a table with Z and A to avoid mixing them up.
In average mass, multiply each mass by its share, add, and divide by 100.
Give one use for each of cobalt-60, iodine-131, uranium-235 and carbon-14.
slides.narration: Some exam tips. Show the electron distribution, then the valency on the next line. For ions, state clearly which electrons were gained or lost. Put isotopes and isobars in a table with the atomic number and the mass number, so that you do not mix them up. In average mass, multiply each mass by its share, add them, and divide by one hundred.

sections.heading: 1. Subatomic particles and how they were found
sections.body_md:
Atoms are divisible. They contain three **subatomic particles**: the **electron** (charge −1, mass about 1/1836 u, outside the nucleus), the **proton** (charge +1, mass 1 u, in the nucleus) and the **neutron** (no charge, mass about 1 u, in the nucleus).

**Electron.** In a discharge tube at low pressure, **cathode rays** leave the cathode. J. J. Thomson (1897) showed that they bend towards the positive plate, so they are negative, and that they are the same for every gas and metal.

**Proton.** Goldstein (1886) found **canal rays**, which pass through holes in the cathode and are positive. With hydrogen the particle is the lightest positive one, the proton.

**Neutron.** James Chadwick (1932) found a neutral particle of about the mass of a proton.

key_terms.definition_md: A particle smaller than an atom: the electron, proton or neutron.
A beam of electrons from the negative plate of a low-pressure discharge tube.
Positive rays that pass through holes in the cathode; with hydrogen they are protons.
The tiny, dense, positive centre of the atom, made of protons and neutrons.

sections.heading: 2. Thomson's and Rutherford's models
sections.body_md:
**Thomson (about 1904):** a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding. The atom is neutral because the charges are equal. It could not explain the gold-foil result.

**Rutherford (1911)** fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through (the atom is mostly empty space), a few were deflected (the positive charge is concentrated) and very few (roughly one in many thousands; books quote figures such as 1 in 8000 or 1 in 12 000) bounced back (a tiny, dense, positive **nucleus** holds almost all the mass). Electrons revolve around the nucleus.

**Limitation:** a revolving charge should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom should not be stable.

key_terms.definition_md: A fast, positively charged particle (a helium nucleus) used in the gold-foil experiment.
Thomson's picture of electrons embedded in a positive sphere.

sections.heading: 3. Bohr's model
sections.body_md:
Bohr (1913): (1) electrons revolve only in certain fixed paths called **shells** or energy levels, K, L, M, N ($n = 1, 2, 3, 4$); (2) an electron **does not radiate energy** while it stays in a shell; (3) each shell has a fixed energy; (4) an electron **absorbs** energy to jump to a higher shell and **emits** energy when it falls to a lower shell.

This removed the problem of Rutherford's model. **Limitation:** the model works for hydrogen but is too simple for atoms with many electrons.

key_terms.definition_md: A fixed path or energy state in which an electron can stay without radiating.
A shell in which an electron does not lose energy.

sections.heading: 4. Electron distribution and valency
sections.body_md:
The shell with number $n$ can hold at most $2n^2$ electrons: K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32. Electrons fill the nearest shell first, and the outermost shell holds at most 8 (2 for K). For the first 20 elements: K 2, L 8, M up to 8, then N.

Examples: Na 2,8,1 (valency 1); Mg 2,8,2 (2); Al 2,8,3 (3); Si 2,8,4 (4); P 2,8,5 (3); S 2,8,6 (2); Cl 2,8,7 (1); Ar 2,8,8 (0); K 2,8,8,1 (1); Ca 2,8,8,2 (2).

**Valency:** 1 to 4 outer electrons gives that number; 5 to 7 gives 8 minus it; a full outer shell (2 in K, 8 otherwise) gives 0.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of electrons in each shell, written for example as 2, 8, 7.
The combining power of an atom, decided by its outer electrons.
The electrons in the outermost shell.

sections.heading: 5. Atomic number, mass number and ions
sections.body_md:
**Atomic number** $Z$ = number of protons (= electrons in a neutral atom). **Mass number** $A$ = protons + neutrons. **Neutrons** $= A - Z$. An atom is written $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$.

An **ion** is a charged atom: protons stay the same. A **cation** has lost electrons (electrons $= Z - \text{charge}$); an **anion** has gained electrons (electrons $= Z + \text{charge}$). Example: $^{27}_{13}\text{Al}^{3+}$ has 13 protons, 14 neutrons and 10 electrons.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
An atom that has gained or lost electrons and so has a charge.

sections.heading: 6. Isotopes, isobars, uses and average atomic mass
sections.body_md:
**Isotopes:** same element (same $Z$), different mass numbers (different neutrons); same chemical properties. Examples: protium, deuterium and tritium; chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. **Isobars:** different elements (different $Z$) with the same mass number, such as argon-40, potassium-40 and calcium-40.

**Uses:** cobalt-60 (treating cancer, sterilising equipment); iodine-131 (thyroid diagnosis and treatment); uranium-235 (nuclear fuel); carbon-14 (dating fossils and old wood).

**Average atomic mass** = sum of (mass number × abundance) divided by 100. Chlorine: $(35 \times 75 + 37 \times 25) / 100 = 35.5$ u.

key_terms.definition_md: Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers.
Atoms of different elements with the same mass number.
An isotope whose nucleus gives out radiation.
The abundance-weighted mean of the masses of the isotopes of an element.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Name the scientist, year and evidence for each discovery, and pair every Rutherford observation with its conclusion.
- Give one limitation for each of the Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models.
- Write the electron distribution first, then the valency from the outer electrons.

cards.front_md: Name the three subatomic particles and their charges.
cards.back_md: Electron (negative), proton (positive), neutron (no charge).

cards.front_md: Where are the protons and neutrons found?
cards.back_md: Together in the nucleus at the centre of the atom.

cards.front_md: What is the mass of an electron compared with a proton?
cards.back_md: About 1/1836 of a proton, so almost zero.

cards.front_md: What are cathode rays?
cards.back_md: A beam of electrons from the cathode of a low-pressure discharge tube.

cards.front_md: How did Thomson show that cathode rays are negative?
cards.back_md: The beam bends towards a positive plate.

cards.front_md: What are canal rays and who found them?
cards.back_md: Positive rays that pass through holes in the cathode; found by Goldstein.

cards.front_md: Who discovered the neutron and when?
cards.back_md: James Chadwick, in 1932.

cards.front_md: Describe the Thomson model of the atom.
cards.back_md: A sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding.

cards.front_md: What did Rutherford fire at the gold foil?
cards.back_md: Fast, positively charged alpha particles.

cards.front_md: Why did most alpha particles go straight through the foil?
cards.back_md: Most of the atom is empty space.

cards.front_md: What did the rebounding alpha particles show?
cards.back_md: A tiny, dense, positive nucleus holds almost all the mass.

cards.front_md: About what fraction of alpha particles bounced back?
cards.back_md: A tiny fraction: roughly one in many thousands.

cards.front_md: State the limitation of the Rutherford model.
cards.back_md: A revolving electron should lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would collapse.

cards.front_md: What does Bohr say about an electron staying in a shell?
cards.back_md: It does not radiate energy while it stays in that shell.

cards.front_md: What happens when an electron jumps to a higher shell?
cards.back_md: It absorbs energy.

cards.front_md: What is the limitation of the Bohr model?
cards.back_md: It works well for hydrogen but is too simple for atoms with many electrons.

cards.front_md: What is the maximum number of electrons in shell n?
How many electrons can the outermost shell hold at most?
cards.back_md: 8 (2 for the K shell).

cards.front_md: Electron distribution of sodium (Z = 11)?
Electron distribution of chlorine (Z = 17)?
Electron distribution of potassium (Z = 19)?
How do you find valency from outer electrons?
cards.back_md: With 1 to 4 outer electrons, valency equals that number; with 5 to 7, it is 8 minus that number; a full outer shell gives 0.

cards.front_md: Valency of oxygen? Of argon?
cards.back_md: Oxygen 2 (2,6); argon 0 (2,8,8).

cards.front_md: Define atomic number.
cards.back_md: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

cards.front_md: Define mass number.
cards.back_md: The number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus.

cards.front_md: How do you find the number of neutrons?
cards.back_md: Mass number minus atomic number, A − Z.

cards.front_md: How many electrons has a cation of charge 2+?
cards.back_md: Z − 2, because the atom lost two electrons.

cards.front_md: What are isotopes? Give an example.
cards.back_md: Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers, such as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

cards.front_md: What are isobars? Give an example.
cards.back_md: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number, such as argon-40 and calcium-40.

cards.front_md: Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties?
cards.back_md: They have the same number of electrons and the same outer electrons.

cards.front_md: Name one use each of cobalt-60, iodine-131, uranium-235 and carbon-14.
cards.back_md: Cancer treatment; thyroid disorders; nuclear fuel; dating fossils and old wood.

cards.front_md: How do you find the average atomic mass of an element?
cards.back_md: Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage, add, and divide by 100.

questions.stem_md: In a discharge tube, a glowing beam passes between two charged metal plates and is pulled towards the plate that carries a positive charge. This shows that the beam:

options.text_md: is made of positively charged particles
is made of negatively charged particles
is made of particles with no charge
is a beam of light, which charges cannot bend

questions.solution_md: Unlike charges attract. A beam pulled towards the positive plate must carry negative charge, so these particles (electrons) are negative — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Alpha particles are fired at a thin metal foil. A tiny number come straight back, although almost all the others pass through. This is best explained by saying that:

options.text_md: the positive charge and most of the mass of an atom are packed into a very small nucleus
the atom is a solid sphere with charges spread evenly through it
electrons in the atom are heavier than the alpha particles
the foil is too thick for alpha particles to pass through

questions.solution_md: Only a head-on meeting with a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus can turn a fast alpha particle back. Option (a) states this. A solid evenly charged sphere would not turn back any alpha particle.

questions.stem_md: Rutherford's model failed because an electron circling the nucleus should lose energy and fall in. Which idea of Bohr removes this objection?

options.text_md: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons
Electrons are embedded in a positive sphere
An electron in a fixed shell does not radiate energy
Alpha particles can bounce back from a foil

questions.solution_md: If an electron radiates no energy while it stays in a shell, it has no reason to spiral inwards. This is Bohr's postulate, option (c). The other statements belong to other models or experiments.

questions.stem_md: Goldstein used a cathode with holes in it. The rays that came out behind the cathode were called canal rays. These rays:

options.text_md: carry a negative charge and move in the same direction as cathode rays
carry a positive charge and move in the direction opposite to cathode rays
carry no charge and are not affected by a magnet or by plates
are a beam of electrons that have gained energy

questions.solution_md: Gas atoms in the tube lose electrons and become positive. The positive particles move towards the cathode, pass through the holes, and travel the opposite way to cathode rays — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student draws the Thomson model of the atom. Which description of her drawing is correct?

options.text_md: A small positive centre with electrons moving in circles outside it
A large negative sphere with small positive protons inside it
A set of fixed shells with electrons that jump between them
A positive sphere with small negative electrons scattered inside it

questions.solution_md: Thomson's model has a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it, as in option (d). Option (a) is Rutherford's picture and option (c) is Bohr's.

questions.stem_md: Chadwick found a new particle in the nucleus in 1932. Which property made it harder to find than the electron or the proton?

options.text_md: It has no electric charge, so plates and magnets do not deflect it
It is much lighter than an electron
It carries a negative charge of two units
It is found outside the nucleus

questions.solution_md: Charged particles can be bent by electric or magnetic fields and so are easier to trace. The neutron has no charge, which made it difficult to detect — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A nitrogen atom has 7 protons, 7 neutrons and 7 electrons. Almost all of its mass is in the nucleus because:

options.text_md: electrons have no mass at all
protons and neutrons are lighter than electrons
the electrons are held far outside the atom
an electron is about 1800 times lighter than a proton or a neutron

questions.solution_md: Each electron has only about 1/1836 of the mass of a proton, so the 14 nucleons carry almost all the mass — option (d). Electrons do have a very small mass, so option (a) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: In Bohr's model, an electron in a sodium atom drops from the M shell to the L shell. During this change, the atom:

options.text_md: gives out energy
takes in energy
neither takes in nor gives out energy
loses a proton

questions.solution_md: A lower shell has less energy. An electron falling to it gives out the difference in energy — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Rutherford's experiment, almost all the alpha particles passed through the gold foil without being deflected.

**Reason (R):** Most of the volume of a gold atom is empty space.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true, and R is true. The empty space lets the particles pass straight through, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Bohr's model, an electron that moves in a shell keeps radiating energy and slowly falls into the nucleus.

**Reason (R):** An electron jumps to another shell when it absorbs or emits a fixed amount of energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: in Bohr's model an electron in a shell does not radiate energy. R is true: jumps between shells involve fixed amounts of energy — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In Rutherford's model, the electrons are packed inside the nucleus with the protons.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons; the electrons revolve outside it, in the empty space.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A neutron has nearly the same mass as a proton but carries no electric charge.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. A neutron is neutral and has a mass of about 1 u, almost the same as that of a proton.

questions.stem_md: The particle with no charge that was found in the nucleus by James Chadwick is the ___.
questions.solution_md: Chadwick discovered the **neutron**.

questions.stem_md: In the Bohr model, the shell that lies closest to the nucleus is called the ___ shell.
questions.solution_md: The shell with $n = 1$ is the **K** shell.

questions.stem_md: Why were the rays that appear behind the cathode of a tube with a perforated cathode called canal rays, and what charge do they carry?

answer.model_answer_md: The rays pass through holes, or canals, in the cathode, so they were named canal rays. They are made of positive particles, formed when gas atoms lose electrons, so they carry a positive charge and move opposite to cathode rays.

questions.solution_md: Pass through canals (holes) in the cathode; positive charge.

marking_scheme.step: Named because they pass through holes (canals) in the cathode

questions.stem_md: A student says that an electron moving around a nucleus must lose energy and fall into it. Which idea of Bohr answers her, and why do atoms last?

answer.model_answer_md: Bohr said that electrons move only in certain fixed shells and do not radiate energy while they stay in one. Because an electron in a shell loses no energy, it does not spiral into the nucleus, and the atom stays stable.

questions.solution_md: Stationary shells without radiation; so the electron stays in its shell and the atom is stable.

marking_scheme.step: Electrons move only in fixed shells and do not radiate energy there
So they do not spiral inwards and the atom is stable

questions.stem_md: A copper wire is made of atoms that contain protons and electrons, yet the wire does not shock you when it is not connected to a battery. Explain why a normal atom is neutral.

answer.model_answer_md: A normal atom has as many electrons as protons. Each electron carries the same amount of negative charge as a proton carries positive charge, so the charges cancel. Neutrons carry no charge, so the atom as a whole has no net charge.

questions.solution_md: Equal numbers of protons and electrons; equal and opposite charges cancel.

marking_scheme.step: Number of protons equals the number of electrons
Equal and opposite charges cancel, and neutrons have no charge

questions.stem_md: Describe the Thomson model of the atom. Name one observation that this model could not explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge spread evenly through it, with electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding. The total positive and negative charges are equal, so the atom is neutral. The model could not explain why a very few alpha particles bounce back from a thin gold foil, as no concentrated positive centre exists in it.

questions.solution_md: Positive sphere with embedded electrons; neutral; fails to explain rebounding alpha particles.

marking_scheme.step: Positive sphere with electrons embedded in it
Equal positive and negative charge, so neutral
It could not explain alpha particles bouncing back from a gold foil

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe how Rutherford carried out his alpha-particle scattering experiment.

(b) Give three observations and the conclusion drawn from each.

(c) State one limitation of the model he proposed.

answer.model_answer_md: Rutherford directed a narrow beam of fast, positive alpha particles at a very thin gold foil and used a screen around it to see where they went. Most particles passed straight through, so most of the atom is empty space. A few were deflected through small angles, so the positive charge is concentrated in a small region. Very few, roughly one in many thousands, bounced back, so this region, the nucleus, is tiny, dense and holds nearly all the mass. His model could not explain why an electron circling the nucleus does not lose energy and spiral into it.

questions.solution_md: Set-up; three observation-conclusion pairs; instability of the electron orbit.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Alpha beam at thin gold foil, observed on a screen
(c) Revolving electron should lose energy and fall in

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the postulates of Bohr's model of the atom.

(b) Explain how the model removes the main difficulty of Rutherford's model.

(c) What happens to the energy of an atom when an electron jumps to a shell farther from the nucleus?

answer.model_answer_md: Bohr proposed that electrons revolve only in certain fixed paths called shells (K, L, M, N), each with a fixed energy, and that an electron does not radiate energy while it stays in its shell. Rutherford's electron should have lost energy and spiralled into the nucleus. Since an electron in a shell does not lose energy, it stays in its shell and the atom is stable.
